Regularly considering sex differences within local data, alongside disability, ethnicity, sexual orientation, age and deprivation, can help areas identify where there is the greatest unmet need and target action more effectively.

Platforms such as Fingertips and Spotlight bring together hundreds of indicators on population health, health inequalities, risk factors, behaviours, service uptake and outcomes, allowing users to compare local areas with regional and national benchmarks, where available. The LG Inform men’s health report (published 2026) provides a valuable source of local intelligence, enabling local authorities to explore and compare progress against a range of indicators and identify opportunities to target support where needed. Local data sources such as healthcare or locally commissioned service data may also provide more timely information that can be used for local needs assessments.

Local partners can consider where gaps in data limit understanding of men’s health outcomes, experiences or service use, and whether existing data collection and reporting arrangements could be used or adapted to support more effective planning, commissioning and service delivery. For example, where appropriate and proportionate, considering sex-disaggregated reporting on outcomes within contracts can provide understanding of what is working.

Partners can also work with community organisations run for men to help organisations build the evidence base for their contribution to health and wellbeing outcomes.

Further examples of how local systems can use data and insight are included throughout this guidance.

Governance and accountability

Local system leaders have a crucial role in driving progress on men’s health. By providing clear governance, senior ownership and accountability, they can help embed men’s health within existing priorities. This section provides examples of how men’s health can be built into governance, planning and performance arrangements.

ICBs and NHS providers

NHS organisations have statutory duties to reduce health inequalities, including duties relating to gender and sex. Health inequalities are defined as avoidable differences in health outcomes between groups or populations - such as differences in how long we live, or the age at which we get preventable diseases or health conditions.

In line with the Core20PLUS5 approach, NHS organisations are encouraged to draw on data and intelligence from a range of sources to build a robust understanding of men’s health and wellbeing needs across the life course, including how these vary between population groups and places. This can build on existing integrated needs assessments, joint strategic needs assessments (JSNAs) and neighbourhood health plans.

At a minimum, performance, quality and outcomes data can be disaggregated by sex, age, ethnicity and deprivation, and embedded in routine reporting to identify inequalities in access, experience and outcomes, including across relevant indicators within the NHS Oversight Framework.

Quantitative data could be combined with qualitative and community insight data to understand the barriers that may prevent men from accessing or engaging with care, including digital exclusion, transport barriers and the accessibility and flexibility of services.

These insights can help to establish a clear starting point and inform strategic commissioning decisions and measurable improvement plans, with progress tracked against relevant outcome goals to determine whether healthcare inequalities are reducing.

Combined strategic authorities

Combined strategic authorities can use their strengthened health duties to address the structural drivers of men’s health inequalities, while ensuring alignment with related agendas, such as jobs and skills growth and healthy workplaces. Operating across a wider geography can help authorities bring together data and insight on groups of men whose needs may be harder to understand or respond to within a single local authority. Their role can include:

convening partners

aligning action on employment, skills, transport and housing with local health priorities

supporting delivery through existing local services

Local authorities

As the local authority’s statutory source of public health expertise, directors of public health can play an important role in informing local priorities and supporting evidence-based action. Directors of public health can use reports including the JSNA, specific in depth needs assessments, and their annual directors of public health reports to raise awareness of men’s health issues, highlight local inequalities and stimulate action across the wider system. Local authorities are encouraged to ensure that recommendations from these reports are implemented and monitored through the HWB.

Elected members can play an important role in scrutinising local system progress from neighbourhoods to across the authority and its partners. The Local Government Association’s Must know: supporting men’s health guidance supports councillors to encourage officers and partners to understand local needs.

The health scrutiny committee also provides a more formal opportunity to investigate how well system partners are addressing men’s health inequalities and review performance.

Health and wellbeing boards (HWBs)

The convening role of HWBs can also be a useful vehicle for accountability on men’s health. HWBs can look at how men’s health is considered in the JSNA and in the subsequent strategies developed by partners, including neighbourhood delivery plans. Part of this could also consider the involvement and engagement of local men as well as analysis of sex and gender differences when designing commissioning and delivery models of services.

HWBs may also consider whether a local men’s health or gender equality plan could be needed to accelerate and co-ordinate action.

Practical examples include:

identifying, connecting with and amplifying local community organisations that support men’s health, including by promoting their services through local networks and strengthening referral routes into them

creating a range of opportunities for men to connect through sport or other activity-based provision, including practical opportunities such as cooking, building or nature-based activity, or creative opportunities such as singing, dance, painting or theatre

raising awareness of the support offered through social prescribing and considering how to link men with local services that can support their individual practical, social or emotional needs

considering the Department for Media, Culture and Sport’s social connection framework to identify and support boys and young men at risk of loneliness and isolation in the design and delivery of services

ensuring fathers are involved in the design and delivery of services through Best Start Family Hubs and Healthy Babies, as set out in the local authority guidance and sharing best practice examples through the Healthy Babies father-inclusive practice professionals network

encouraging family support services to offer parenting programmes and activities for fathers and contacting fathers in their own right instead of defaulting to them as secondary parents

considering the support needs of the partners of women who access perinatal mental health services, with suitable pathways and referral processes available for father and co-parent specific support

embedding father-inclusive practice across the system of family support services through workforce training and clear strategic commitments

Case study: integrating support for fathers and families in Norfolk

Locally collected data in Norfolk identified low awareness and uptake of perinatal mental health services among fathers. There was also limited collaboration between the Parent-Infant Relationship Service (PAIRS) and the Perinatal Mental Health Service (PMH), and referrals to PAIRS had declined following the COVID-19 pandemic.

In response, Norfolk County Council worked to integrate pathways for both services through their family hubs service, enabling families to access the right support regardless of where they first made contact. This included co-locating provision within family hubs, increasing workforce capacity and training staff to identify families’ needs and refer them to appropriate support. Father-inclusive practice training was delivered to 95 people across the local workforce.

Norfolk also invested £135,000 to fund community and voluntary sector organisations to provide place-based social activities for fathers as part of the PAIRS and PMH pathway. Local fathers participated in a multi-agency panel that assessed bids and decided which organisations received funding.

Norfolk reported that referrals to PMH services increased by 33% in 2023 to 2024 compared with the previous year. Referrals for fathers and co-parents increased by 60%, compared with 28% for mothers. The 95 participants in the father-inclusive practice training rated their level of knowledge and confidence before and after attending. On average, their ratings increased by 54% and 37% respectively.

Addressing societal norms

The Men’s Health Strategy recognises that norms are not driven by individual men but by the rules, relationships and incentives within different settings - such as schools, workplaces and healthcare environments - which shape what is acceptable, expected or difficult for men. These norms, roles and expectations often influence whether men find it harder to acknowledge their concerns, speak about their issues or seek help. These expectations also shape how services recognise and respond to men’s needs and whether men who seek help feel listened to and receive appropriate support. Norms can and do change, and local systems can play a critical role in shifting harmful societal norms towards healthier alternatives.

Practical examples include:

avoiding masculine stereotypes that assume what men might prefer or need from support and instead directly engaging with target groups to ask them their views

building on the motivations, assets and strengths that matter to men, using service design and communications to support positive behaviours and help-seeking, rather than reinforce harmful norms, particularly around mental health

using images and language that reflect the diversity of men’s experiences and backgrounds, and considering how sex and gender intersect with age, ethnicity, disability, faith and sexual orientation

reviewing local policies, services and professional practices to identify and address factors that may unintentionally reinforce harmful norms, for example, expectations to work through illness or distress, or processes that make it harder for men to disclose concerns

Tackling the greatest health challenges and conditions

This section provides examples of targeted action which can be taken to tackle the major contributors to premature mortality and inequalities among men. These include actions on conditions such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and respiratory disease as well as challenges such as suicide - which remains one of the leading causes of death for men under the age of 50. National data from the Office for National Statistics highlights that the highest rates of suicide among men in England are in the North East, South West, Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West. Local data and insight can help identify which groups of men have the greatest unmet need and inform where activity is focused.

Practical examples include:

reviewing access and retention within mental health support, including mental health neighbourhood centres, with a concentration on sex and gender and intersectionality, to ensure pathways meet the needs of those at highest risk of suicide, self-harm and poor mental health

The guidance outlines the foundations for local action, including governance, accountability, data and insight, and provides a practical checklist to help organisations get started. It then explores each of the strategy’s 6 levers for action, outlining why they matter and providing practical examples and case studies that can be adapted to local contexts.

Introduction

In November 2025, the government published England’s first Men’s Health Strategy, setting out a long-term vision to improve the health and wellbeing of all men and boys.

The strategy made a clear case for action. Men continue to experience poorer outcomes across a range of health issues and are more likely to die prematurely from preventable causes. In 2025, 35% of all deaths among men in England were before the age of 75. On average, men living in the most deprived areas of England are expected to die more than 10 years earlier than those living in the least deprived areas and spend significantly fewer years in good health. Rates of cancer, circulatory and respiratory conditions drive much of this difference in life expectancy. Men also account for around three-quarters of deaths by suicide and are more likely to experience a range of risk factors that can harm health and wellbeing, including smoking, harmful gambling, alcohol consumption and substance misuse. Men can also face barriers to seeking help and engaging with services, meaning opportunities to prevent ill health can be missed.

These outcomes reflect:

the places where men live, learn and work

the relationships and communities around them

wider social, economic, environmental and cultural factors

Addressing these poor health outcomes requires a concerted effort across the whole system.

Since publication of the Men’s Health Strategy, there has been strong interest from local and regional partners in how they can support its delivery. Local authorities, integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS organisations, voluntary and community organisations, employers and many other partners have a critical role to play in designing services, shaping environments and supporting communities in ways that improve men’s health.

Much of this work is already underway. Across England, local systems are developing innovative approaches that support the ambitions of the strategy. Following engagement with a range of health system partners, academics and broader stakeholders, this guidance has been developed to support and share good practice.

Local action is most effective when it is shaped by the men it aims to support. Partners are encouraged to engage directly with men, particularly those experiencing the poorest outcomes, to understand their experiences, needs and priorities, and to help ensure services and interventions are relevant, accessible and effective.

Purpose of this guidance

This non-statutory guidance brings together practical suggestions and case studies to support systems to implement the ambitions of the Men’s Health Strategy. It is for local partners to decide how to use the guidance, based on their own needs and priorities. The suggestions illustrate how men’s health can be considered through existing responsibilities, services and activity. This guidance is aimed at:

health and wellbeing boards (HWBs)

ICBs

local authorities, including directors of public health

primary care networks

NHS providers

It also supports collaboration with voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) organisations that are critical partners for improving population health. The guidance may also be useful for wider local system partners, including:

employers

local businesses

education providers

other public services

Further guidance and resources developed by the men’s health sector that can support local implementation can be found on our men’s health resource hub (login required).

Implementation will look different across England, reflecting local needs, inequalities and priorities. In the 10 Year Health Plan, the government set an overall goal to halve the gap in healthy life expectancy (HLE) between the richest and poorest regions, while increasing it for everyone. Taking action that reflects the needs of local populations is essential to realising the ambitions within the national strategy. Local partners can tailor their approach to the needs of their communities, with particular consideration given to men experiencing the poorest health outcomes and greatest inequalities.

The map uses Middle-layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs), showing inequalities both between and within regions and local areas. Figure 1 shows variation in HLE at birth for males in England, displayed at neighbourhood level. The highest (78.3 years) is found in Westminster in London and the lowest (47.7 years) is found in Stockton-on-Tees in the North East.
